name: Thymosin Fraction 5

lead: Thymosin fraction 5 is a calf-thymus extract made in 1972 by Allan Goldstein's group, containing dozens of peptides. Thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were later purified from it. It matters to this wiki as the origin of peptides that people use for recovery and healthier ageing.

The extract restored immune function in thymus-deficient animals, which led to the idea of thymic hormones. Clinical work focuses on purified thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) in infection and cancer, not on the extract for appearance.

paras: It is rarely used directly; people in thymic-peptide discussions generally use the purified peptides instead.
No approved use of the extract was found, and no appearance-related safety data. Animal-derived mixtures vary in composition.

angle.text: Thymosin fraction 5 is the calf-thymus extract from which thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were purified. It shows up in thymic-peptide discussions as the source of those peptides; no appearance use is documented.

lead: Thymosin fraction 5 (TF5) is a partially purified extract of calf thymus prepared in 1972 by Allan Goldstein's group, which contains many small peptides, including the later-characterized thymosin alpha-1 and thymosin beta-4 [1][2][3][1]. It was the starting material from which individual thymosins were purified, and it was tested in patients before the purified peptides existed.

Its relevance to looksmaxxing is as a root of the thymic peptide family. Thymosin beta-4 and thymosin alpha-1 are the forms that appear in recovery, longevity and research-peptide discussions, where people hope for faster tissue repair and better immune resilience, which supports training and general appearance over time. Published clinical work focuses on purified thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) in infection and cancer, not on TF5 for appearance [4][5].
The extract itself is no longer a typical consumer product, and no approved use of crude TF5 was found.

paras: Work on thymic extracts began in the 1960s with Abraham White and then Allan Goldstein, who showed that extracts restored immune function in animals lacking a thymus [2][6]. Goldstein, a biochemist who later chaired biochemistry at George Washington University from 1978 to 2009, co-discovered the thymosins with White [7]. TF5 was reported to contain over 40 peptides of roughly 1,000 to 15,000 daltons, grouped as alpha, beta and gamma thymosins; they are structurally unrelated, and some are widespread in tissues rather than thymus-specific [6].

A 2018 paper in Expert Opinion on Biological Therapy re-evaluated TF5 after 35 years using high-resolution mass spectrometry, revisiting what the original fraction really contains [8]. Later reviews describe beta-thymosins as a family of actin-binding proteins with intracellular and extracellular activities [9][10].

Thymosin alpha-1 was isolated and sequenced in 1977 and 1979 [3][11][12], and bovine thymosin beta-4 was sequenced in 1981 [1]. Later work found that alpha-1 derives from a larger precursor, prothymosin alpha [13].

Thymosin alpha-1 was isolated and sequenced in 1977 and 1979 [3][11][12], and bovine thymosin beta-4 was sequenced in 1981 [1]. Later work found that alpha-1 derives from a larger precursor, prothymosin alpha [13]. Wikipedia's biography of Goldstein reports that thymosin alpha-1 was the first thymosin to enter clinical trials and is approved in China and more than 30 other countries, and that thymosin beta-4 has been studied for wound healing in ulcers and dry eye, with an injectable form under development by RegeneRx Biopharmaceuticals, where Goldstein is chief scientific advisor [7].

Thymic hormones were studied as a link between immune aging and endocrine function. A 1999 review of the thymus-pituitary axis reviews reports that TF5, thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 affected beta-endorphin, ACTH, glucocorticoid, LHRH and LH secretion in animal and cell models, and that aging changes pituitary responsiveness to thymic hormones [14]. A 1981 Science paper reported that thymosin stimulated luteinizing hormone-releasing factor secretion [15]. Reviews in the 1980s examined thymosins and the immunology of aging [16]. These strands underlie the longevity interest, but they are laboratory and review-level observations.

sections.h: Research use in cancer and transplantation
paras: A Cochrane review of randomized trials of purified thymus extracts and synthetic thymic peptides alongside chemotherapy or radiotherapy in adults with cancer identified 26 trials with 2,736 patients; 20 tested extracts (thymostimulin or thymosin fraction 5) and six tested synthetic peptides (thymopentin or thymosin alpha-1) [17]. A 1983 study reported that TF5 did not accelerate reconstitution of immune reactivity after human marrow grafting [18], and a 1988 report followed patients who received thymic grafts or factors after marrow transplantation for 2 to 12 years [19].

TF5 itself is not a typical consumer product; purified peptides derived from it, chiefly thymosin alpha-1 and thymosin beta-4, are what appear in research-peptide markets and in recovery and longevity discussions. Thymosin alpha-1 is an approved drug in China and other countries under the name thymalfasin, according to Goldstein's biography [7]. No approved use of the extract was found.

No studies of crude TF5 as an appearance intervention were found. Clinical research on thymic preparations includes the Cochrane meta-analysis of 26 cancer trials, of which most tested extracts such as TF5 or thymostimulin [17]; a placebo-controlled pilot trial of thymosin in chronic hepatitis B in 1991 [20] and a review of thymalfasin for that disease [21]; and a clinical-trial review of thymic hormones in patients with phobic disorders [22]. Registered phase 2 trials test thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) in cancer settings, including pneumonia prevention in lung cancer (n=69), advanced refractory solid tumors and metastatic esophageal cancer [4][5][23]. Laboratory work also reported effects of thymic hormones on natural killer cell activity [24].
